question: How does this chip get made, and who can make it?
title: Semiconductor Manufacturing: A Practical Reference
lede: A leading-edge chip takes something like a thousand process steps, and the hardest ones run on tools that one or two companies in the world know how to build. This guide covers {{N_ENTRIES}} technologies across seven stages, from the bare wafer to the tested package, with the tool costs, node economics, and supply concentration that decide who gets to make what.

facets.label: Device
facets.tip: What the technology is mainly used to build. Directional rather than exhaustive: most front-end steps touch several device types, and the tag marks where the choice actually gets argued about.

facets.label: Node
facets.tip: Process generations the technology is used at. Mature = 28 nm and above · Advanced = 16–7 nm · Leading = 5–3 nm · Frontier = 2 nm and below. Packaging and test entries carry the nodes of the dies they handle, and compound-semiconductor entries sit at Mature because those devices are built with 1990s-era lithography.

facets.label: Wafer
facets.tip: Substrate format the step runs on: Small = 150 mm and below · 200 mm · 300 mm · Panel = the rectangular formats used in packaging. Die cost scales with usable area per substrate, so a platform stuck on 150 mm pays several times more per mm² than one on 300 mm. Untagged where the step happens on singulated packages rather than a substrate.

facets.label: Tool cost
facets.tip: List price of the most expensive single tool the capability requires: <$1M · $1–10M · $10–100M · $100–250M · $250M+. New Western list prices; used tools and Chinese-built equivalents run well below them, and a fab buys dozens to hundreds of each.

facets.label: Suppliers
facets.tip: How many firms can supply the critical tool or material at production quality today: Sole source (1) · 2–3 firms · 4–8 firms · Many. This is the axis that decides who can be cut off, by an export-control regime or by a single fire at a single plant.
